stem:
A 30-year-old woman who is 35 weeks pregnant attends the maternity assessment unit because she has not felt the baby move since yesterday evening. The midwife cannot find the fetal heart with a handheld Doppler. Her blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg and she has no abdominal pain or vaginal bleeding.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Cardiotocography to look for a fetal heart rate trace
options.B: Repeat handheld Doppler auscultation in one hour
options.C: Real-time ultrasound scan to look for fetal cardiac activity
options.E: Start induction of labour with misoprostol

correct_answer: C. Real-time ultrasound scan to look for fetal cardiac activity
why_correct: Suspected intrauterine fetal death should be confirmed as soon as possible using two-dimensional real-time ultrasound to demonstrate absent fetal cardiac activity. A second suitably trained practitioner should confirm the diagnosis where possible. Out of hours, a practitioner with appropriate training may use a portable ultrasound machine. Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 55, Care of Late Intrauterine Fetal Death and Stillbirth (2nd edition, 2024).
why_wrong: A. A CTG can record the maternal heart rate and cannot confirm or exclude fetal death. B. Waiting delays the diagnosis; ultrasound should be done straight away. D. There is no maternal indication for emergency caesarean, and fetal death has not been confirmed. E. Induction is not started until fetal death is confirmed and the woman has been counselled about her options.
pearl: Only ultrasound confirms fetal death. A handheld Doppler or CTG can mislead by picking up the mother's pulse.
thinking: No fetal movements + no heart on handheld Doppler  ↓  do not rely on Doppler or CTG  ↓  real-time ultrasound of the fetal heart, ideally with a second operator.
exam_trap: Choosing CTG because it is the usual next test for reduced fetal movements when a heartbeat is present.
takeaway: Confirm suspected intrauterine death with real-time ultrasound, not Doppler or CTG.

stem:
A 28-year-old woman who is 33 weeks pregnant has an intrauterine fetal death confirmed on ultrasound. She is well, with normal observations. Her blood group is O RhD positive. A full blood count, clotting screen and group and save have been sent.

Which additional blood test should be offered?

options.E: No further test, because she is RhD positive

why_correct: A Kleihauer test is offered to all women after intrauterine fetal death, not only those who are RhD negative, because fetomaternal haemorrhage can be a cause of fetal death. It should be taken as early as possible, before birth, so that a fetomaternal haemorrhage is detected before it clears. In RhD-negative women it also guides the dose of anti-D. Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 55, Care of Late Intrauterine Fetal Death and Stillbirth (2nd edition, 2024).
why_wrong: B. Beta-hCG has no diagnostic role once fetal death has been confirmed on ultrasound. C. CA-125 has no role in investigating fetal death. D. A thrombophilia screen is no longer offered to all women at diagnosis; it is considered selectively once the placental pathology report is available. E. The Kleihauer test is offered regardless of RhD status, because fetomaternal haemorrhage is a cause of fetal death in its own right.
pearl: The Kleihauer test after stillbirth is about finding a cause, not only about anti-D dosing.
thinking: Confirmed intrauterine death  ↓  look for a cause  ↓  feto-maternal haemorrhage is one  ↓  Kleihauer test for every woman.
exam_trap: Assuming the Kleihauer test is only for RhD-negative women.
takeaway: Offer a Kleihauer test to all women after intrauterine fetal death, whatever their RhD status.

stem:
A 32-year-old woman who is 37 weeks pregnant has an intrauterine fetal death confirmed on ultrasound. She reports a watery, offensive vaginal loss for two days. Her temperature is 38.7°C, heart rate 118 beats per minute and blood pressure 104/66 mmHg.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Give oral mifepristone and allow her home, to return in 48 hours
options.B: Give intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics and expedite birth on the labour ward
options.C: Expectant management with full blood count and clotting checked twice weekly
options.D: Give oral antibiotics and await spontaneous labour
options.E: Book an elective caesarean section for later in the week

correct_answer: B. Give intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics and expedite birth on the labour ward
why_correct: This woman has suspected maternal sepsis in the setting of intrauterine fetal death. She needs urgent assessment and treatment for sepsis, including intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics, appropriate cultures and blood tests (including a clotting screen), with urgent birth on the labour ward once stabilised. Sepsis is not a situation for expectant management at home. Urgent birth is also needed for abruption or antepartum haemorrhage and severe pre-eclampsia. Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 55, Care of Late Intrauterine Fetal Death and Stillbirth (2nd edition, 2024).
why_wrong: A. Going home is reasonable only when the woman is well; this woman is septic. C. Expectant management is unsafe with sepsis and ruptured membranes. D. Oral antibiotics are inadequate for suspected sepsis, and waiting for labour delays source control. E. Delay is unsafe, and vaginal birth is recommended for most women after fetal death.
pearl: Sepsis, abruption and severe pre-eclampsia turn intrauterine death into an emergency.
thinking: Intrauterine death + fever + tachycardia + offensive loss  ↓  probable chorioamnionitis / maternal sepsis  ↓  IV antibiotics + urgent birth on labour ward.
exam_trap: Following the routine pathway (mifepristone and home) without recognising sepsis.
takeaway: After intrauterine death, sepsis, abruption or severe pre-eclampsia mean urgent birth, not expectant care.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman has an intrauterine fetal death confirmed at 36 weeks. She is well, her blood pressure is normal and her membranes are intact. After counselling, she chooses to go home and wait for labour to start on its own, which may take several days or longer.

What monitoring should be arranged while she waits?

options.A: Full blood count and clotting screen twice weekly

correct_answer: A. Full blood count and clotting screen twice weekly
why_correct: If birth is delayed for more than 48 hours after fetal death, the full blood count and clotting screen should be repeated twice weekly, because the risk of maternal coagulopathy (disseminated intravascular coagulation) increases the longer the fetus is retained. She should also receive clear safety-netting advice and return immediately if she develops fever, bleeding, abdominal pain or feels unwell. Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 55, Care of Late Intrauterine Fetal Death and Stillbirth (2nd edition, 2024).
why_wrong: B. Repeated scans do not detect the main maternal risk, which is coagulopathy. C. CTG monitors the fetal heart, which has no role after fetal death. D. Expectant management needs planned review and blood monitoring. E. Monthly renal tests do not monitor for disseminated intravascular coagulation.
pearl: The longer the delay after fetal death, the higher the risk of maternal DIC.
thinking: Fetal death + expectant management beyond 48 h  ↓  risk of maternal DIC  ↓  FBC and clotting twice weekly.
exam_trap: Thinking expectant management needs no follow-up because the fetus has already died.
takeaway: If birth is delayed more than 48 hours after fetal death, check FBC and clotting twice weekly.

stem:
A woman gives birth in hospital in England to a stillborn baby at 26+3 weeks of pregnancy. The baby showed no signs of life at birth. The birth was attended by a doctor and a midwife, and there are no suspicious circumstances.

Which statement about certification and registration is correct?

options.A: The doctor issues a medical certificate of cause of death, and the death is registered within 5 days
options.B: The birth does not need to be registered because the baby never breathed
options.C: A medical certificate of stillbirth is issued, and the stillbirth must be registered within 42 days
options.D: The stillbirth must be referred to the coroner before it can be registered
options.E: Registration is needed only if a post-mortem examination is performed

correct_answer: C. A medical certificate of stillbirth is issued, and the stillbirth must be registered within 42 days
why_correct: A baby born dead from 24+0 weeks is a stillbirth. A doctor or midwife present at the birth, or who has examined the baby after birth, issues a medical certificate of stillbirth, and in England and Wales the parents are normally responsible for registering the stillbirth within 42 days. Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 55, Care of Late Intrauterine Fetal Death and Stillbirth (2nd edition, 2024); Births and Deaths Registration Act 1953; Still-Birth (Definition) Act 1992; GOV.UK, Register a stillbirth.
why_wrong: A. A medical certificate of cause of death is for deaths after a live birth, not stillbirths. B. Stillbirths from 24+0 weeks must be registered. D. Stillbirths are not routinely referred to a coroner simply because they are stillbirths. E. Registration is a legal requirement whether or not a post-mortem is done.
pearl: From 24+0 weeks, a baby born dead needs a medical certificate of stillbirth, not a death certificate. The 42-day limit applies in England and Wales; in Scotland it is 21 days.
thinking: Born without signs of life at ≥24+0 weeks  ↓  stillbirth  ↓  medical certificate of stillbirth from an attending doctor or midwife  ↓  parents register within 42 days (England and Wales).
exam_trap: Choosing the medical certificate of cause of death, which applies only after a live birth.
takeaway: Stillbirth from 24+0 weeks: medical certificate of stillbirth, then registration (normally by the parents) within 42 days in England and Wales.

stem:
A 31-year-old woman had a stillbirth at 36 weeks two days ago. Pre-eclampsia was diagnosed at the time of birth and her blood pressure today is 158/102 mmHg on oral treatment. She asks for help to stop her breast milk coming in.

What is the most appropriate advice?

options.C: Supportive measures such as a well-fitting bra, simple analgesia and avoiding breast stimulation, without a dopamine agonist
options.D: A combined oral contraceptive pill to suppress lactation
options.E: Restrict her fluid intake until lactation stops

correct_answer: C. Supportive measures such as a well-fitting bra, simple analgesia and avoiding breast stimulation, without a dopamine agonist
why_correct: This woman has persistent hypertension (158/102 mmHg) after pre-eclampsia. Cabergoline is generally preferred for lactation suppression after stillbirth, but the MHRA states that cabergoline and bromocriptine should not be given to women with hypertension or pre-eclampsia. Supportive measures such as breast support, simple analgesia and avoiding breast stimulation should therefore be used here. Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 55, Care of Late Intrauterine Fetal Death and Stillbirth (2nd edition, 2024); cabergoline (Dostinex) SmPC; MHRA Drug Safety Update, bromocriptine (October 2024).
why_wrong: A. Cabergoline is contraindicated in pre-eclampsia and should not be used in postpartum hypertension; serious events including hypertension, stroke, myocardial infarction and seizures have been reported in postpartum women. B. Bromocriptine is contraindicated in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, including pre-eclampsia, and in postpartum hypertension (MHRA Drug Safety Update, October 2024). D. Oestrogen is not used for lactation suppression and raises venous thromboembolism risk after birth; combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC 4 within 21 days of birth. E. Fluid restriction does not suppress lactation and can cause harm.
pearl: Cabergoline is generally preferred for lactation suppression, but it should not be given to women with hypertension or pre-eclampsia. Check blood pressure before prescribing.
thinking: Stillbirth + wants lactation suppressed  ↓  cabergoline is usual  ↓  but pre-eclampsia with high BP  ↓  MHRA: no dopamine agonist  ↓  supportive measures.
exam_trap: Reaching straight for cabergoline without checking for hypertension or pre-eclampsia.
takeaway: Check blood pressure before offering cabergoline; do not give a dopamine agonist to a woman with hypertension or pre-eclampsia.
